1:
The date and the title occupy three of them. Adam Clarke reports that the psalm is untitled in the Hebrew, the Chaldee and the Vulgate, while the other versions give it to Haggai and Zechariah, and places it after the captivity, when the Jews were rebuilding. He adds the fact that explains the numbering of the whole book: every version but the Chaldee breaks the psalm at the eleventh verse and begins a new one at the twelfth, so that the count catches up with the Hebrew, having until now run one behind. John Calvin gives the same list and the same ascription, though he names the second author Zephaniah while the Greek words he quotes name Zechariah; he cites a bishop who called it a thanksgiving of the returned captives, Keil and Delitzsch want no title at all: the tone is that of the restoration period, and they set out the arrival of the priest with about two thousand exiles and of the cup-bearer thirteen years later.

On why the praise is called good, each takes a different ground. Augustine of Hippo refuses to let the goodness rest in the singing: the tongue praises but for a while, and the life must praise ever; and a psalm is not any song but a song to an instrument, so that the singer accompanies his voice with his hands. C.H. Spurgeon hears the whole book ending in a cataract of praise, and prefers singing with heart and voice to singing in the heart alone, since it lets others join. Matthew Henry divides it: pleasant, because holy joy is the principle of it and praising God is work that is its own wages; and comely, since in giving honour to God we do ourselves honour. Calvin turns it into a rebuke of the near-universal weariness at the very mention of God. Charles Ellicott alone looks at the words rather than the duty, and cannot decide whether the poet altered a line of an earlier psalm on purpose or whether the text should be corrected to match it.

The building and the healing separate the spiritual reading from the historical. John Gill takes the city for the church, of which Christ is the builder, the ministers instruments and the people materials, and the broken in heart for those whom the physician alone can cure, pouring in oil and wine as the good Samaritan. Ellicott stays with the philology: build up means rebuild, and the word for outcasts is the one a prophet uses of the dispersion after the captivity, rendered dispersion by two ancient versions and those thrust out by a third. Clarke reports that the psalmist appears to see the walls rising under his eye, and traces the word for broken to a root meaning to break in pieces, from which our own word shiver comes. Henry adds that some outcasts made themselves so by their own folly, and are gathered by being given repentance.

The stars draw the fullest comment. Gill notes that the ancient astronomers pretended to tell them and fixed the number at a thousand and some odd, counting only such as commonly appeared; since the use of telescopes many more are seen, and the clusters of the Milky Way cannot be told at all. He adds a Jewish interpreter’s thought that the outcasts are scattered over the earth as the stars over the upper orb, and he who knows the one knows the other. Ellicott finds the reference abruptly introduced but the train of thought clear, hearing behind it the promise to Abraham and a prophet’s call to lift the eyes and behold. Henry makes them soldiers, mustered and marshalled and coming and going at command. On the meek they are briefest: Gill fills a column with the marks of humility, while Clarke and Ellicott each gloss the word in three words as the afflicted.
7:
The verb rendered sing is really answer, and four of them make four things of it. Adam Clarke takes it as a direction for performance: sing responsively, in parts, answering one another. John Gill agrees, and adds a Jewish authority for reading the first clause of vocal and the second of instrumental music. Charles Ellicott reports the same literal sense and that some think it suggests an antiphonal arrangement, but is more interested in the join: the strophic arrangement is only loosely marked, yet the psalm takes a new departure here with a fresh call to praise and fresh proofs from nature. C.H. Spurgeon makes it devotional — God speaks to us in his works, and our lives should be responses to his love — and then declares himself on the instrument. Under a dispensation of ritual, he says, music was commendable in the great congregation; those who judge it less desirable in public worship now, because of its abuses, still rejoice in it in private, and it is a profanation that choice minstrelsy should be given to unworthy themes.

On the clouds Gill turns meteorologist and then preacher. He explains them as exhalations of vapours out of the earth and of waters out of the sea, drawn up by the sun and let down in showers in the proper places; then he makes them an emblem of afflictive providences, a day of clouds and thick darkness when the Lord hides his face and our sins interpose, grievous and not joyous but tending to make the saints more holy. Clarke keeps to the providence, observing that the direction of the winds and the collection of the clouds are alike under particular management, and stops to record a loss: five ancient versions add a half-line about herb for the service of man which has dropped out of the Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch pass over the weather entirely, noting only that in the Greek the section beginning at the twelfth verse stands as a psalm by itself.

The ravens draw out the tenderness. John Wesley explains why they are named: they were the most contemptible of birds, unclean to the Jews, and are not only neglected by men but forsaken by their dams as soon as they can fly, so that they are left wholly to providence. Gill argues upward from them, that the beasts cannot provide for themselves but wait upon God, and that he will much more feed his own people; and he adds the sting that in their fallen state his people are become like the beasts, which they own when grace calls them. Ellicott draws the moral, that toward one as great to grant as mighty to make the proper attitude is not conceit of wisdom and strength but humble dependence.

The horse and the legs puzzle only one of them. Clarke reads the pair as the two things men most admire, the horse for beauty and strength and fleetness, and a man’s legs, if well proportioned, more than the finest features of his face. Gill makes it military, a horse prepared for battle being a vain thing for safety, and a mounted troop a pleasing sight that raises expectations and is of no account with God. Wesley disposes of it in a line, as if God needed either to accomplish his designs. Ellicott alone calls the antithesis strange: it has been explained of cavalry and infantry, but a plainer passage was before this poet and would hardly have been altered so; and since Eastern nations take fleetness of foot as the mark of a vigorous warrior, he finds the best explanation in the standing epithet of the swift-footed Achilles. Clarke ends the section by dividing the book, holding that the preceding psalm ends here in all the versions but the Chaldee and that these are two distinct psalms referring to different periods.
12:
The city addressed is not the same city in every hand. John Gill stacks three Jewish authorities and takes none of them literally: one refers the call to the inhabitants, a second to the days of Messiah, a third to the spiritual city, which Gill makes the Gospel church, free, and the mother of us all. Matthew Henry keeps the stones but sorts the singers, letting the inhabitants praise God in their own houses while the priests and Levites who attend in the city of their solemnities praise him in a special manner, since with them it is a business and a profession. C.H. Spurgeon presses the same division into an epigram, that the city of peace should be the city of praise, and adds that we are to praise in our own houses as well as in his house. Charles Ellicott looks only at the verb, and reports that it properly means to stroke or to soothe.

The strengthened bars divide them along the same line. Adam Clarke reads them as a date: earlier in the psalm the walls were still going up, here they are finished and provisions brought in, so that the grain was in safety. Ellicott thinks an allusion to the new fortifications probable but holds the expression plainly figurative of security and peace. John Wesley cuts under both in a line, that their strength consisted not in walls and gates and bars but in his protection. Henry says it at more length: they kept their gates barred in times of danger, but that was no security unless God fortified their fortifications, and we should attribute the repose of a land more to the wall of fire than to the wall of water round about it. Gill takes the gates and bars for the security of the church against sin, law, Satan, the world, death and hell, with angels for guards about her. Spurgeon turns it on his own century: modern libertines would tear down all gates and abolish all bars, but so do not we, because of the fear of the Lord; and he wishes our churches as well preserved from false doctrine and unholy living.

On the blessed children two of them agree that this is the real fortification. Henry says the increase of a people strengthens the bars of its gates as much as anything, and that it is a comfort to the generation going off to see the rising one numerous and hopeful. Spurgeon makes the same pairing, that internal happiness is as truly the gift of God as external security, and ends with the turn that when God makes thy walls salvation thy gates must be praise.

The peace and the wheat are read historically, figuratively and spiritually at once. Clarke names the neighbours who had stopped troubling them, the Samaritans and the Moabites. Henry distinguishes peace in the borders from peace upon them, the first got by composing differences so that there are no intestine animosities, the second by preventing invasion; and since the frontier towns lie most exposed, peace in the borders is universal peace. Gill divides it three ways, the outward peace of the church with her enemies, the concord of her members, and the inward peace of conscience that comes of believing. Ellicott renders the clause as placing peace for thy border, and notes that the finest of the wheat is literally the fat of wheat. Henry makes the most of that: the land was enriched not with precious stones nor spices but with the best wheat, which it exported abroad, and it was bread that strengthens the heart of man which made it the glory of all lands. Keil and Delitzsch set out the remaining verses in a single block of text and add not one word of comment on any of them.
15:
What the commandment is draws four answers from one of them alone. John Gill reports a Jewish authority who makes it the rain, since snow and frost follow; a second who makes it the decree of God executed on earth; and the Targum, which makes it the essential Word, the Messiah, who came when the fulness of time was come. Gill himself prefers the word of the Gospel and the sending of the apostles into all the earth. Adam Clarke keeps the personification without deciding: it is the substantial word, an active agent running everywhere and performing the purposes of his will. John Wesley makes it sufficient without any instruments. Charles Ellicott sees a messenger who runs out first to bind the earth up with frost and then to release it, and guesses that some extraordinary season of frost kindled the poet, so that he not only elaborates his model but improves on it.

At the snow the reading becomes anthology. Gill collects the ancients who called snow woolly water, a Latin epigrammatist who called it a thick fleece of waters, another poet who called the clouds flying fleeces, and a naturalist who called it the foam of the celestial waters; then he turns it useful: as wool covers the sheep, so snow covers the earth and keeps the wheat safe from the cold. Ellicott quotes the same Latin line, and adds a traveller who reports that there the snow falls in flakes the size of a walnut and looks more like locks of wool than it does in ours. Clarke says only that nothing in nature has a nearer resemblance to fine white wool. Wesley extends the likeness to use, the snow keeping the fruits of the earth warm, and presses the second comparison further: the hoar frost is like ashes in colour and smallness of parts, and also in its burning quality.

On the ice they divide into the theological and the meteorological. Gill takes the morsels for hailstones and remembers where hail has fallen before, in one of the plagues and on the Canaanites in the days of Joshua, with a great storm yet to come, so that the verse is expressive of the judgments of God. Ellicott glosses morsels as crumbs and says the allusion is doubtless to hail. Clarke answers the question who can stand before his cold from the crusading chroniclers: one records that on an expedition against Mount Tabor in December many of the poor people and beasts of burden died of it, and another that thirty of those attending Baldwin near the Dead Sea were killed by horrible hail and unheard-of snow; the winters in that country, he concludes, are often very severe. At the thaw he and Gill name the same agents, the sun breaking out or the rain falling in plenty and the warm south wind, so that the waters flow where the ice bound them.

The turn from the weather to the law is noticed by three of them. Gill marks it as the passage from nature to grace, and gives his usual double reference: the Targum reads it of the law, given only to the posterity of Jacob, but the word of grace is included too, and was first published to the Jews. He adds that it had to be shown, since its things are hidden from the natural man and could never be discerned without a revelation. Clarke states the claim flatly, that to no nation of the world beside had God given a revelation of his will. Ellicott sets the same movement in the structure, since in each piece into which the psalm divides the thought passes from the grandeur of God in nature to the favour granted to Israel; and he corrects one word, the judgments of the last verse being plainly not manifestations of wrath but the display of righteousness.
